blocks.text: You already know a NumPy 1D array cold from the last module: a fixed sequence of values, all the same dtype, indexed by plain integer position starting at zero. A pandas Series is that exact same idea with one addition bolted on. It is a one dimensional array of values, plus an explicit label for every single position. That label is called the index, and it is what turns a raw block of numbers into something you can actually reason about, like "sales on Monday" instead of "the value at position 3".

blocks.alt: A Series built from a NumPy array of values with index labels attached to each slot
blocks.caption: A Series is a NumPy array with labels riding alongside every value.

blocks.text: Under the hood, a Series is genuinely just a NumPy array with an index object sitting next to it. Pandas is built directly on top of NumPy, so every trick you already learned there, dtypes, vectorized math, broadcasting, carries straight over. This lesson is about what that label layer buys you, how to build a Series three different ways, how to grab values out of it by label or by position, and one alignment behavior that will genuinely surprise you the first time you hit it.
1. What A Series Actually Is

Picture a single column pulled out of a spreadsheet. It has a bunch of values stacked vertically, and it has row labels running down the left edge, whether those are row numbers, dates, or names. That is a Series. Pandas describes it as a one dimensional labeled array, and both halves of that phrase matter equally.

items: One dimensional: a Series holds a single sequence of values, not a grid. For a full table with many columns, you want a DataFrame, which the next lesson covers.
Labeled: every value has an index label sitting next to it, and that label is how you ask for the value back later.
Array: the values themselves live in a real NumPy array underneath, with a single shared dtype, exactly like the arrays you built in the NumPy module.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

prices = pd.Series([120, 145, 98, 210])
print(prices)
# 0    120
# 1    145
# 2     98
# 3    210
# dtype: int64

blocks.text: Notice the two columns printed there. The left column, 0 through 3, is the index. The right column is the data. Ask pandas for prices.index and prices.values separately and you will get an Index object and a plain numpy.ndarray back, respectively. That is not a coincidence or an abstraction pandas is hiding from you, that ndarray really is the same array class you spent the whole last module on.

blocks.title: Why this connects back to NumPy
blocks.content: Every Series is backed by a NumPy array for its values. That means dtype rules, vectorized operations, and broadcasting from the NumPy module all apply here unchanged. A Series adds exactly one new thing on top: labels.

blocks.text: 2. Creating A Series Three Ways

Pandas lets you build a Series from a list, a dict, or a single scalar, and each starting point behaves slightly differently once the index gets involved. Knowing which one to reach for saves you from writing extra lines of setup code later.
2.1 From A Python List
The simplest path is a plain list. Pandas takes the values as they are and attaches a default index automatically, counting up from zero.

code.content:
temps = pd.Series([21.5, 22.0, 19.8, 23.1])
print(temps.index)   # RangeIndex(start=0, stop=4, step=1)
print(temps.values)  # array([21.5, 22. , 19.8, 23.1])

blocks.alt: A Python list feeding into a Series with a default RangeIndex attached automatically
blocks.caption: Build from a list and pandas hands you a RangeIndex for free.

blocks.text: That default index behaves exactly like NumPy positional indexing, so if you never pass an explicit index, a Series from a list feels almost identical to a plain 1D array with a bit of printed decoration around it.
2.2 From A Dict

This one is worth slowing down on, because it is genuinely useful and a little different from what you would expect coming from NumPy. When you build a Series from a dict, the dict keys automatically become the index, and the dict values become the data.

code.content:
population = pd.Series({'Mumbai': 20961000, 'Delhi': 30291000, 'Bangalore': 12765000})
print(population)
# Mumbai       20961000
# Delhi        30291000
# Bangalore    12765000
# dtype: int64

blocks.alt: A Python dict of key value pairs feeding into a Series where the dict keys become the index labels
blocks.caption: Dict keys walk straight into the index, no extra step needed.

blocks.text: This is the fastest way to get a genuinely meaningful index without writing it out separately. Instead of remembering that city number 2 is Bangalore, you just ask for population["Bangalore"] directly.
2.3 From A Scalar
You can also build a Series from a single scalar value, as long as you also hand pandas an index to broadcast that value across. The scalar gets copied to every single label you provide.

code.content:
default_stock = pd.Series(0, index=['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'])
print(default_stock)
# apple     0
# banana    0
# cherry    0
# dtype: int64

blocks.alt: A single scalar value and a given index feeding into a Series where the scalar is broadcast to every label
blocks.caption: One scalar value, copied out across whatever index you hand it.

blocks.text: This pattern shows up constantly when you need to initialize something, a running total per category, a default flag per row, before filling in real values later.

blocks.title: A quick rule of thumb
blocks.content: List gives you values first and a default index second. Dict gives you both values and index at once, tied together by key. Scalar gives you one value repeated across an index you supply yourself.

blocks.text: 3. The Index: Default Versus Custom

Every Series has an index whether you asked for one or not. The question is only whether that index is the plain auto generated RangeIndex, 0, 1, 2, and so on, or something you actually chose on purpose.
3.1 The Default RangeIndex

If you do not pass an index, pandas gives you a RangeIndex, which behaves an awful lot like plain NumPy positional access. It is cheap, it is automatic, and it is fine for throwaway data or anything where order is the only thing that matters.
3.2 A Custom Meaningful Index
Pass your own index and suddenly the Series can be looked up the same way you would describe the data out loud. Dates, names, product ids, whatever actually identifies each row in your head.

blocks.alt: A default RangeIndex of plain integers next to a custom index of dates names or ids
blocks.caption: Same values, two very different indexes: counting position versus a label you actually recognize.

blocks.text: The difference is not just cosmetic. With a default RangeIndex, "give me row 1" only tells you a position, and you have to go count to know what that row means. With a custom index, "give me 2026-01-02" tells you exactly what you are asking for, and the code reads like the problem you are actually solving.

blocks.title: A gotcha worth flagging early
blocks.content: A custom index does not have to be unique. Two rows can share the same label. Pandas will let you do it, and a lookup by that repeated label hands back every matching row instead of one. It is rarely what you want by accident, so keep your index unique unless you have a specific reason not to.

blocks.text: 4. Accessing Values: .loc Versus .iloc

Once a Series has a custom index, you need two different ways to reach into it: one keyed by the label itself, and one keyed by plain integer position, the same position based access you already know from NumPy. Pandas gives you both through two accessors, .loc and .iloc. There is a whole dedicated lesson coming up on indexing, so this is just enough to get you moving now.

code.content:
sales = pd.Series([120, 145, 98], index=['2026-01-01', '2026-01-02', '2026-01-03'])

sales.loc['2026-01-02']   # 145, looked up by the label itself
sales.iloc[1]              # 145, looked up by integer position, same row either way

blocks.alt: loc looking up a Series by label and iloc looking up the same Series by integer position, both landing on the same value
blocks.caption: Two doors into the same room: loc walks in by name, iloc walks in by position.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Accessor","What it uses","Works even with a custom index"],"rows":[[".loc","The label as you defined it","Yes, that is the whole point"],[".iloc","The integer position, counting from 0","Yes, position always works regardless of labels"]]}

blocks.title: When to reach for which
blocks.content: Use .loc when you know what the row is called. Use .iloc when you only know where it sits, for example "give me the last three rows" regardless of what their labels happen to be.

blocks.text: 5. Vectorized Operations On A Series

Because a Series is backed by a real NumPy array, every elementwise operation you learned in the vectorization and broadcasting lessons just works here without a single change in mental model. Add a number to a Series and it gets added to every value at once, no loop required, no ufunc call written out by hand.

code.content:
prices = pd.Series([120, 145, 98, 210])

discounted = prices * 0.9
print(discounted.values)   # array([108. , 130.5,  88.2, 189. ])

print(prices > 100)
# 0     True
# 1     True
# 2    False
# 3     True
# dtype: bool

blocks.alt: A NumPy ndarray underneath a Series feeding vectorized elementwise math that runs at full NumPy speed
blocks.caption: A Series inherits every bit of the underlying array’s vectorized speed, it just adds labels on top.

blocks.text: Comparisons, arithmetic, boolean masks, all of it. If it worked on a bare NumPy array, it works on a Series holding the same numbers, and it runs at the same speed under the hood because it genuinely is the same compiled code doing the work.
6. The Alignment Gotcha: Operations Between Two Series

Here is the one behavior in this lesson that catches almost everyone off guard the first time. When you add two Series together, pandas does not line them up by position the way NumPy would with two plain arrays. It lines them up by index label first, matching label to label, and only then does the math.
6.1 When The Indexes Match
If both Series share the exact same index, alignment is invisible, everything just adds up the way you would expect.

code.content:
a = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=['x', 'y', 'z'])
b = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=['x', 'y', 'z'])

print(a + b)
# x    11
# y    22
# z    33
# dtype: int64

blocks.alt: Two Series sharing the exact same index x y z adding cleanly with every label matched
blocks.caption: Same labels on both sides, so addition just works label by label.

blocks.text: 6.2 When The Indexes Do Not Match

Change the index on one side and the entire result changes shape. Pandas still lines things up strictly by label, and any label that only appears on one side gets a NaN in the result, because there is nothing on the other side to add it to.

code.content:
a = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=['x', 'y', 'z'])
c = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=['y', 'z', 'w'])

print(a + c)
# w     NaN
# x     NaN
# y    22.0
# z    33.0
# dtype: float64

blocks.alt: Two Series with mismatched indexes x y z versus y z w producing NaN wherever a label is missing on either side
blocks.caption: The gotcha in one picture: mismatched labels turn into NaN, not a shifted or truncated result.

blocks.text: Notice two things happening at once here. First, only the shared labels, y and z, get a real numeric result, everything else becomes NaN. Second, the dtype quietly changed from int64 to float64, because NaN cannot be represented as an integer, so pandas widens the whole Series to hold it.

blocks.title: Why this trips people up
blocks.content: Coming from NumPy, you would expect pandas to just add the two arrays position by position, the way plain arrays do. It does not. Alignment by label is a deliberate design choice, and it means a mismatched index is a silent source of NaN, not an error. Always check that two Series share the index you think they do before combining them.

blocks.text: 7. Useful Series Attributes
A handful of attributes come up constantly once you start actually working with Series objects rather than just building toy examples.

blocks.alt: A Series object with four attributes hanging off it: values, index, name, and dtype
blocks.caption: The four attributes you will reach for again and again.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Attribute","What it gives you"],"rows":[[".values","The underlying NumPy array holding the raw data, no index attached"],[".index","The Index object holding the labels"],[".name","An optional name for the whole Series, useful once it becomes a DataFrame column"],[".dtype","The single shared data type of every value in the Series"]]}

code.content:
sales = pd.Series([120, 145, 98], index=['2026-01-01', '2026-01-02', '2026-01-03'], name='units_sold')

print(sales.values)   # array([120, 145,  98])
print(sales.index)    # Index(['2026-01-01', '2026-01-02', '2026-01-03'], dtype='object')
print(sales.name)     # units_sold
print(sales.dtype)    # int64

blocks.text: That .name attribute looks minor now, but it matters a lot the moment a Series gets pulled out of, or dropped into, a DataFrame, since the name becomes the column header.
8. Worked Example: A Daily Sales Series
Put everything from this lesson together in one small, realistic example: a week of daily sales figures, indexed by date.
8.1 Building The Series

code.content:
import pandas as pd

dates = pd.date_range('2026-01-01', periods=7)
units = [120, 145, 98, 210, 175, 88, 132]

daily_sales = pd.Series(units, index=dates, name='units_sold')
print(daily_sales)
# 2026-01-01    120
# 2026-01-02    145
# 2026-01-03     98
# 2026-01-04    210
# 2026-01-05    175
# 2026-01-06     88
# 2026-01-07    132
# Freq: D, Name: units_sold, dtype: int64

blocks.alt: Three daily sales figures for January feeding into a single daily sales Series indexed by date
blocks.caption: Real dates as labels, real sales figures as the data, one clean Series tying them together.

blocks.text: 8.2 Doing A Couple Of Operations On It
Grab a single day by its actual date, then run a couple of the vectorized operations from earlier on the whole week at once.

code.content:
print(daily_sales.loc['2026-01-04'])   # 210, straight lookup by date

busy_days = daily_sales[daily_sales > 130]
print(busy_days)
# 2026-01-02    145
# 2026-01-04    210
# 2026-01-05    175
# Freq: D, Name: units_sold, dtype: int64

print(daily_sales.mean())   # 138.28571428571428
print((daily_sales * 1.1).round(1))   # a projected ten percent bump, one line, no loop

blocks.text: Every one of those lines works because the Series is, at heart, a NumPy array. The date index is what makes .loc['2026-01-04'] readable instead of you having to remember that it is entry number three.
9. Series Versus A Plain NumPy Array
It is worth pinning down exactly what a Series adds on top of what you already had, and exactly what it does not change.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Trait","Plain NumPy array","pandas Series"],"rows":[["Values stored","A NumPy array","The exact same NumPy array underneath"],["Access by position","Yes, the only option","Yes, through .iloc"],["Access by label","No such concept","Yes, through .loc, backed by the index"],["Vectorized math","Fast, elementwise, ufunc powered","Identical, inherited straight from the array"],["Combining two of them","Lines up strictly by position","Lines up strictly by index label, mismatches become NaN"],["A name attached to the whole thing","No","Yes, via .name"]]}

blocks.alt: A plain NumPy array offering only position compared against a pandas Series offering position plus a label
blocks.caption: Everything you already know about arrays, plus a label layer that changes how lookups and alignment behave.

blocks.text: A Series never asks you to give up anything you already know about NumPy arrays. It only asks you to remember one new rule: once two Series get combined, the index is what decides which values meet each other, not the order they happen to sit in. Keep that rule in your head and a Series is just a friendlier, better labeled array. The next lesson builds directly on this to introduce the DataFrame, which is really just a collection of Series that all share one index.
